did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ezekiel uses the image of a watchman stationed on the land to explain the responsibility of one who gives warning when danger approaches.
Did you know? Anyone who hears the sound of the trumpet but does not take warning is responsible for his own death; but whoever takes warning saves his life.
Did you know? Ezekiel himself is appointed as a “watchman for the house of Israel”: he must hear the word of the LORD and warn the people.
Did you know? The chapter emphasizes that the LORD does not desire the death of the wicked, but that they turn from their evil ways and live.

Did you know? According to the chapter, a person’s former righteousness does not protect him if he turns to wrongdoing, and a person’s former wickedness does not prevent him from living if he turns from his ways.
Did you know? True repentance is also shown through actions: the wicked person must return what he owes, repay what he stole, follow the laws that lead to life, and avoid wrongdoing.
Did you know? The chapter’s concluding principle is: “I will judge each of you according to your ways”—everyone is judged according to his conduct and actions.
Did you know? A survivor from Jerusalem comes to Ezekiel and announces that the city has been struck down; this news confirms the prophecy of destruction that was given earlier.
Did you know? The hand of the LORD was upon Ezekiel on the evening before the survivor arrived, and in the morning, after he came, Ezekiel’s mouth was opened and he was no longer mute.

Did you know? The people listened to Ezekiel and even enjoyed his voice and music, but they did not follow his words; only when the prophecy came true would they recognize that a prophet had been among them.
